speechtext:
Might I say in reply to the hon. member that we of western Canada realize that we are discussing a matter for all Canada, and we are speaking of the conditions we know best when we speak of western Canada. I noticed from the figures of abandonments that have been made from time to time under the British and civilian and soldier settlement schemes that there were 1,072 abandonments in the St. John district, as compared with 1,611 in Calgary, which would indicate that the whole matter needs to be considered in a much more realistic way than it has so far been considered. I have before me, for example, a statement showing that there have been 14,480 abandonments, quit-claims, and so forth, by soldier settlers, civilian settlers and British families from the inception to November 30, 1937. The original number of soldier settlers was 25,017, and the present number is 9,888, so we can see the tremendously high proportion of abandonments. I believe that this legislation, while necessary so far as it goes, does not meet the actual conditions, and the minister and the department and the government should consider this whole matter more realistically than it is being considered at the present time.
I am fully aware that conditions in Ontario are not good. I have a letter, for example, from the municipal chapter of the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire of Toronto, in which, having observed that I spoke on this matter the other day, they draw my attention to the deplorable condition of settlers under these schemes in northern Ontario. Then only a few moments ago we heard from Prince Edward Island. And so, while each of us speaks of conditions that we know in the province from which we come, it is quite obvious from the figures of the department itself that a much more realistic stand has to be taken in connection with this whole matter than is indicated by this legislation. As a matter of fact, forty per cent of the total settlement has been abandoned already, and many of the settlers who remain are remaining there because they do not know what to do if they get off the land.
Soldier Settlement Act

Perhaps I am a little closer to the soldier settlement problem than some hon. members who have discussed it. I am living on a farm out there and have done so for the past twenty-four years. I do not speak as an arm chair farmer; I think those who farm from the arm chair or the office do not know the conditions that exist and the circumstances under which the soldier settler has to get along. I am not speaking simply for the soldier settlers of Alberta or Saskatchewan but for the soldier settlers all across the dominion.
From the inception of this scheme there were in all 25,017 settlers. A number of the men who took up farming were office men who went to work on the land without any previous experience in farming. When those who have had a life experience in farming are not able to make a living at it, we can appreciate how much harder it is for the man without experience.
In a number of cases soldier settler deals were made more for the benefit of somebody's friends than for the benefit of the soldier himself. I have in mind a half-section of land with some stock and implements, not very far from my own farm, which was sold for $8,000. That farm is subject to frost, and while the settler has done his best during all the time he has been on the land, at the present time he owes $13,000 on an original investment of $8,000, and he has paid out what he could since he bought the land in 1919.
The average original loan to soldier settlers was $4,155. As I said before, these loans were taken advantage of by somebody's friends rather than the soldier settler. We know that several poor farms were sold to settlers, and that balky or unsound horses, poor cows and poor second-hand machinery were turned over to settlers at prices that should have bought the best in each class.
At the end of December, 1937, gross advances on loans amounted to $110,945,926.08, and interest charges $30,643,796.76, or a total of $141,589,722.84.
Up to that time the soldier settlers had paid back in principal $37,161,859.12, and in interest $18,996,161.88, or a total of $56,158,021. In addition there were legislative reductions as follows: In principal and interest, $28,351,653.41; losses on resale of security principal, $17,612,419.28, making a total of $45,964,072.69. That does not include loss of interest on resale, the figures for which are not available; nor does it include interest on the 1922 amendment to the act, which is estimated at $10,269,108.87.
Having passed through this period of depression or oppression, whichever you like to call it, from 1929 down to the present time, we find that from January 1, 1931, to December 31, 1937, interest charges on soldier settler loans amounted to $11,606,721.53. Of this amount $3,701,399.79 was cancelled, leaving a total of $7,905,321.74. To this must be added the cast of administration for this period, amounting to $3,445,324.86, or a total of interest and administration costs for the seven years of $11,350,646.60.
May I ask what the hon. member is reading from?
From information supplied by the minister's department.
My hon. friend, I regret, has still failed to make himself clear. Is he reading from a return brought down to the house?

No, I got it direct from the
department. I am giving these figures because in my opinion the legislation under discussion is not adequate. The figures I have given are amounts charged up and we find that the payments during the period amount to: Principal, 85,501,726.83, and interest $4,350,389.93. or a total of $9,852,116.76, which is less than the amount of interest and administration charges during that period.
Coming to the year 1937, we find that the interest charged amounted to 81,280,956.06. The amount cancelled was $548,880.34. That left total interest charges of $732,075.72. Administration costs were 8558,390. The total was $1,290,465.72.
The total amount paid in the calendar year 1932 was: Principal, $779,743.04, and interest 8644,519.78, or a total of $1,424,262.82, which is very little more than the amount of interest and administration charges.
From the inception of the scheme to the end of March 1937, interest charges amounted to $30,643,796.76; administration costs for the same period, $23,765,179.70, or a total of 854,408,976.46. We find that the total amount of principal and interest paid since the inception of the scheme is S56,158,021, or approximately one and three-quarter millions more than the total amount of interest and administration charges.
The original amount of the loan was 84.155. At the end of March 1931, the average settler owed $2,311, or still fifty-five per cent of his original loan. At the end of December 1937, he still owed $2,271. That is to say, there was a reduction during the seven year period of S40, or a net decrease of about $6 per annum after the settler had
Soldier Settlement Act

supported his wife and family. At the end of December 1937, the settlers were in arrears, principal $5,475,608.29 and interest $5,394,202.12 or an average of $1,101, which is approximiately fifty per cent of the amount the average settler still owes on his land.
I do not know how long these settlers will have to continue working in order to clear their farms. When the recruiting officers were around the country in 1914 looking for soldiers they told the recruits that when they came back Canada would take care of them, but we find that the settlers are now taking care of some of our Canadian citizens and some citizens in other countries instead of Canada taking care of them. During the years following the inception of the scheme conditions were so bad that the government saw fit to reduce the debt in 1930 and I suggest that they should realize by this time that conditions since 1930 have become so much more serious that another drastic reduction is necessary.
About a year ago several members of this house had a communication from the Soldier Settlers' Union, with headquarters at Lloyd-minster, Saskatchewan, requesting that certain concessions be made so that if possible the soldiers might be enabled to get out of debt in the near future. Some of the recommendations were:
1.	That our total debt be as it stood after the 30 per cent reduction and henceforth be a nou-interest bearing debt. All payments made since that time to be applied to principal.
2.	In the event of the death of a settler, clear title be given to his widow or dependent next of kin.
3.	A complete revision of the present collection policy of the department.
4.	A plan devised whereby settlers will be enabled to pay off their loans and at the same time maintain a reasonable standard of living.
*
Legislation has been enacted to bring the officials of the soldier settlement department under the civil service, thus providing pensions and security for their old age. Brigadier General A. Ross, C.M.G., D.S.O., in presenting the case for these officials based his appeal on the grounds of their war service followed by their faithful service in the department after the war period. The soldier settler had war service also and were it not for the settlers there would be no department of soldier settlement, yet the settler has no security for his old age, but is instead faced with hopeless and increasing debt.
It would seem that the men for whom Brigadier-General Ross is speaking are enjoying a good living at the present time while the settlers are being treated in such a way as to suggest that to him that hath shall be given, and from him that hath not shall

be taken even that which he hath. The officials of the Soldier Settlers' Union believe that their requests are very moderate and I am inclined to believe that if the government will survey the whole case of soldier settlers they will realize the importance of taking drastic action at this session. Last session we expected that something would be done but, in view of the coronation on May 12, this subject was pigeonholed. I hope that the minister and the government will now do something worth while for the soldier settler.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Time extended for credit on
payments of arrears.

I propose to oppose the passing of this section with all the vigour that the rules and decency of debate will permit. Unfortunately the method of presentation of this bill has been such as to convey an impression which 1 know is quite foreign to the character and intention of the minister-the impression of concealment. I say that quite sincerely. I know the minister is not responsible, but the method by which the bill has been presented has given that impression. When something is brought down by way of resolution in this house and goes out to the public meaning such and so-because after all the English language is interpretable generally along one line-and then when the bill brought down means something entirely different, this promotes dissension. Had the measure brought down given the soldiers concerned more than the resolution indicated there would have been no trouble; but when the legislation provides much less than the resolution indicated, this makes trouble for everyone. I think a large proportion of hon. members and certainly a large number of people throughout the country' took from the resolution the meaning which I did, and which indeed its language conveys. This is how it reads:
.	.	. and to provide further that the period
during which payments of arrears or instalments at present subject to bonus privileges may be made, be further extended.
It does not say extended to the extent of twelve per cent; it says "be extended." To the ordinary man on the street that means extending it to tihe same extent as it was before. I think we are in a sense flouting the governor general's recommendation in this. He recommended certain legislation, but we are doing something else. If logic and argument do not prevail I might think it worth while to move a point of order, that

Soldier Settlement Act
this bill is out of order inasmuch as it does not conform to or is not based upon the resolution as introduced. But let that go for the moment. The minister appears to have trusted a good deal to some conversation he had with someone as to what the legion at their convention thought about the matter. I hold in my hand the February number of the Legionnaire, on page 11 of which is a list of the resolutions, "some of the most important resolutions dealt with," and among them is, "that the dollar for dollar bonus be continued to soldier settlers." That means that it be continued, it does not mean that eight or ten or twelve per cent of it be continued.
Then again we find the minister saying, as reported on page 998 of Hansard, that, after all, things were not so bad; that it is a nice world anyhow, and that the soldier could get relief under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. But we have just passed an act making it possible for any province, apparently at the suggestion of the province, to do away with that act. So that is rather a broken reed.
Not necessarily at the suggestion of the province.
Well, I do not know at whose suggestion; the suggestion of the dominion government, then.

Yes; the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in its application may be suspended or terminated in any particular province by proclamation, but that would only be after all the purposes of the act had been in effect fulfilled. Every person who had made application for adjustment of his obligations under that act would still have his application considered.

According to the language used in the debate, especially by hon. members from Ontario, the desire seemed to be to have that act cancelled at once. That certainly was not consulting the people who wanted to come under it; some hon. members seemed to be more concerned with those people who would be affected from the creditor's point of view. But we have passed an act making it possible for the dominion government at a moment's notice to cancel that act, and therefore the relief that the minister indicated the settlers might get in that way is extremely visionary.
There are two objections to this section, apart from the method of bringing it in, which could perhaps be remedied by taking the bill out and bringing in another resolution. But the two fundamental objections to this bill wherein it is unfair to the settler,
are these: The old dollar for dollar bonus was allowed to any settler, whether he was in arrears or not when he made a payment on account of his indebtedness, be that indebtedness back interest or back instalments, or current interest oi current instalments; he got 82 credit for every SI he paid. And that is what the soldiers and settlers thought they were going to get when they saw this resolution brought down. Now it appears that they are going to get not that, but something which may apply to approximately one-third of them. Then there is a further deduction which I shall deal with in a moment. But the first patent injustice, as it seems to me to be, is that the bill is going to apply not to all settlers, but only to a limited few, somewhere about one-third. A man who scraped and saved and took the money out of the children's bank or the money his wife had inherited to pay right up, with some idea of pride, thinking, "For once we will show the government that I have paid up"; the man who paid his obligations right up to date, is not going to get any more relief. But the man who said, "Oh, well, the government must carry me. I will go and buy a car, or a radio, and let some of it lie back," is going to get the benefit of the dollar for dollar system. That is a wrong state of affairs, because it puts a premium on the man who hangs back and does not do what he can, something which we have not hitherto done in these transactions.
Well, that was bad enough. However, for the moment we swallow that; we have to. But there is a further thing which I noticed only to-day-and I must compliment whoever drew the amendment upon the subtle way in which it is worded. You do not see the nigger in the wood-pile until you study not only the language of the section itself but the explanation on the opposite page of the bill. You will notice it says:
The total of bonusable indebtedness is not increased.
Why do they not say it is going to be very largely decreased? Why not be frank? Then they go on to say "as heretofore," which means, "as before", or "according to what has been done in the past."
As heretofore, only such amounts as were due and payable before April 1, 1938, may be repaid on the bonus basis.
It is true they say, "due and payable before April 1, 1938"; but they use the words "as heretofore."
Now a further detriment to these unfortunate people who come within this abbreviated and curtailed bonus system is this: A great many of us thought they would at least
Soldier Settlement Act

continue to get the same advantages as under the old system. Does the explanation not say, "as heretofore"? They were allowed to get dollar for dollar for eveiything they paid on arrears of interest or capital or instalments due. One would think the settlers who were going to get this advantage would get that advantage too. But this is not so. You find that they get the dollar for dollar bonus only on the payment past due April 1, 1938. On the payment due in April or October, 1938, although the payment for April may be in arrears, they get no rebate. So that the amount we are giving them is very small indeed.
I am going to test the feeling of the committee-more to put the matter in concrete form so that it will be seen what it is and what it should be-by moving the following amendment:
That after the word "arrears" in line 1 on page 2 the words "or of any instalment" be inserted, and in the second line the figures "1938" be struck out and the figures "1941" be inserted.
So that it would then read:
73 (1) Any settler or person indebted in respect of any contract or agreement made prior to the first day of January, 1933, under the provisions of this act, who after the thirty-first day of March, 1933, makes payment on or before the thirty-first day of March, 1941, in respect of any arrears or of any instalment due and payable before the first day of April, 1941, shall, subject to the provisions of this section, receive credit toward payment of such arrears for a further sum equal to the payment made.
I think that carries out the absolute spirit of the resolution as introduced, at least as we read it, and also the spirit of fairness as regards the past, as well as having regard to the possibilities of the settlers; for, as someone said just now, we are talking about whether the interest on taxes paid and insurance should be seven per cent or five per cent, but what does this matter, when you are not going to get it anyhow, or have to cut it down very seriously? This would keep alive the promises made by the minister two years ago when he introduced this. I raised the question then of extending it for five years, and he said no; two years was enough, and if the same conditions prevailed two years later he would again renew it. This has not been done, though to all intents and purposes the conditions are the same. I shall move that amendment, just to put the matter in concrete form in order to show the difference between what is in this bill and what, in my humble opinion at least, should be in the bill.

I cannot agree with the position taken by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. The adequacy-or inadequacy, which my hon. friend thinks is the better term- of the resolution was pretty well discussed when the resolution was before the house.
It was discussed but it was not explained.

I have gone further into the matter, and there is no doubt in the opinion of the law advisers who drafted the resolution that it is full enough and broad enough to cover the bill which was introduced subsequent to the adoption of the resolution by the house.
But the bill does not cover the resolution. That is the trouble.
My hon. friend is now rather reversing his position. At first he stated that he was criticizing the resolution.
Oh, no.

I do not, of course, wish to misrepresent my hon. friend, but I submit that the resolution is in conformity with the bill; or I shall put it the other way, that the bill is in conformity with the resolution. At the same time I admit that probably the resolution might have been a little more clearly drafted, but I would direct the attention of the committee to the wording of the resolution, which states:
That it is expedient to amend the Soldier Settlement Act for the purpose of reducing from seven per centum to five per centum the interest rate charged on certain repayments to the board of taxes and insurance premiums paid by the board in respect to soldier settlement lands in case of default on the part of the settler-
This is the important part:
-and to provide further that the period durir^ which payments of arrears or instalments at present subject to bonus privileges-
That is, in connection with all those arrears of interest or instalments of principal which up to the 31st of this month are subject to bonus privileges, the bill proposes that the soldier settler who has not been able to take advantage of that provision may have an opportunity to do so within the next three years. I think that is quite clear. As I said a moment ago, it may be that the resolution could have been more clearly drafted, but I submit that it is sufficient for the purposes of the bill.
May I direct the attention of the committee to one other point. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni drew in contrast the picture of the returned man who had been frugal and saving, and who had made his payments.

Soldier Settlement Act
Well, he obtained the advantage of the dollar for dollar bonus privilege up to March 31, on all his payments and all his interest arrears. That fact cannot be disputed. It is equally true that, if this legislation passes, he does not have that privilege beyond March 31. Now take the case of the other man, at the other end of the stick, who perhaps may have been in a position to take advantage of the dollar for dollar bonus privilege but who bought a car or went on a trip or did something else instead. In connection with those portions of his payment in arrears, both principal and interest, up to March 31, he can still claim the dollar for dollar privilege, but he cannot get that bonus on the payments that fall due after March 31 of this year. So in that respect he is on precisely the same footing as the frugal soldier settler who sacrificed creature comforts, let us say, in order to take advantage of the bonus. This does not discriminate as between them; it simply extends, very largely because of the drought condition in western Canada, to those soldier settlers who, because of crop failure, sickness or some other reason, have not been able to take advantage of the bonus privilege up to the present time, the opportunity to do so for another three years. I submit to the committee that this is reasonable and fair legislation.
May I add one further word. It is comparatively easy to exhibit a generous attitude of mind as far as the returned men are concerned. I find no fault with that, but I think the consensus of opinion-I am taking reasonable opinion in Canada-not only among our civilian population but among the vast returned soldier population, is that the returned soldiers have not asked and are not asking any special favours, except in the occasional odd case that one may expect to find. What they want is reasonably fair treatment, and I again point out to the committee the fact that I mentioned a little earlier in the afternoon. The returned soldiers who settled on the land, who took advantage of the offer of the government during the period immediately following the war, in a sense have been in a preferred position as compared with other returned men.
I recall the purpose of the legislation passed at that time. The hon. member for Comox-Albemi was not in the house when1 this legislation was passed. I was in the house, and I recall the discussion that took place. There was a good deal of opposition to the establishment of this system of returned soldier land settlement. At that time it was pointed out by some hon. members that precisely the evils or the difficulties which have arisen in the course of administration would arise. It was
pointed out that there would be perhaps a vary small minority of returned men who would feel that the country ought to do everything possible for them. But for good or for ill the plan was adopted. The vast majority of those who joined the Canadian expeditionary force, according to my information almost ninety-eight per cent, have not benefited through this soldier settlement scheme. There were numerous instances-I think every hon. member knows of them- of returned men who established themselves without the advantage of any assistance. Perhaps they were more enterprising; perhaps they had more of the spirit of independence and self-reliance, which unfortunately I think is going into a decline in this country to-day, than those who took advantage of the settlement scheme. Is it to be opened up so that those men will get some advantages also? Take the man who established himself in a small business. He has not had assistance from the government. I think on the whole this legislation and its administration must be tested on the basis of whether or not the treatment of the returned men who went on the land has been fair. I believe the whole record, from 1920 down to the present date, supports the view that it has been fair.

Up to date, yes.
Mr. CRERAR- I think that is the view of the great majority of returned men. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni quoted from a journal as to the opinion of the legion respecting the extension of the privilege right across the board. I have not the resolution with me; but my information is-and I think it is correct-that the legion at its recent meeting at Fort William, passed a resolution which was practically on all fours with the principle embodied in the present legislation. For that reason I regret I cannot accept the amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.
As I understand the matter, the effect of the bill is that there will be no dollar for dollar bonus on any payments falling due after April 1, 1938.
Correct.
But there will be a privilege given to those who are in arrears with payments already due of making those payments on the dollar for dollar basis until April 1, 1941?
Yes, they have three years in which to do so.

I believe the dollar for dollar bonus was initiated in 1933. At that time it was intended to last for a period of three
Soldier Settlement Act

years. Then, in 1936 this parliament passed an amendment extending the time for a further two years. It seems to me the test as to whether or not that period should now be exended again is this: What are the conditions in agriculture in Canada at the present time? This afternoon we have heard about distress in the prairie provinces, in Prince Edward Island and in northern Ontario. I know there is great hardship among some of the soldier settlers in British Columbia. Suggestions have been made that the soldier settlers should take advantage of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act which, after all, is not as satisfactory a procedure as getting consideration under the Soldier Settlement Act. We have also heard the suggestion made that interest should be waived, and that other concessions be made.
I put it to the minister earnestly that conditions in Canada are not yet ripe for cancelling the dollar for dollar bonus. We have not yet reached that stage. I suggest to him that although he may not accept the amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, he should himself bring in an amendment to the act which will extend for a reasonable period the time during which the soldier settlers may take advantage of the dollar for dollar bonus.

The hon. member for Comox-Alberni stated what, in my opinion, is a definite and true fact. It was my intention to bring the attention of the committee to the wording of the bill. I am inclined to think the impression has gone abroad that people were going to take advantage of the dollar for dollar bonus. It would appear that the purpose of the bill is simply to give an opportunity to those people who have arrears due to take advantage of the measure. The individual whose instalments will be due later on will not enjoy the same privileges. I cannot understand why a man whose payments come due a year or two after the amendment comes into effect should not have the same privilege as one whose instalments are already due. As one hon. member has said, conditions in Canada do not warrant discrimination of this kind simply because of the dates upon which payments may fall due.
I support the view taken by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and I believe that in this measure the government is not meeting the desire of the people, and is not meeting what the people were led to believe they could expect on the passing of the legislation. Therefore I strongly support the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.

When the
measure was before the house on another occasion I protested against the way in which the resolution had been drafted, and the way in which it was being interpreted. However, the resolution was accepted, and the legislation is now before us. I still think the resolution was drawn either carelessly or craftily. I do not know which term to use.
I hold in my hand figures which will illustrate what I mean by saying that many men had paid up their instalments, with considerable difficulty to themselves, and that others who had not paid and who were living in the same district were now going to have the benefit, over a longer period of time. This means that they will be able to have the use of money, for their own purposes, over a long period of time, at the expense of the government.
In three subdistricts of northern Saskatchewan with which I am familiar, and which I believe beyond the shadow of a doubt were the subdistricts in the best condition of any part of that province last year, the total, including arrears, due last fall, amounted to $314,380.33. The actual payments made totalled $41,255.01, or about twelve and a half per cent of the amount due. The number of settlers with payments due stood at 546. Of that number I find that 138 paid in full and that 161 paid in part. It would appear, therefore, that almost one-quarter of the settlers with accounts due paid in full, and nearly one-third paid in part. But by that number, comprising almost two-thirds of the settlers with payments due, only about one-eighth of the amount of money due was paid back. So that those who did not pay anything owed the great bulk of the $314,380.33. This condition has been going on for some time, and these people have had the use of the money. They live in the same district with the 138 people who paid in full. That money has been in use for a long time, and for the next three years they will continue to enjoy it at a rate of two and a half per cent. I say that, because the interest having been cut to five per cent, and the bonus payments being due on a fifty-fifty basis, the use of the money will cost two and a half per cent for interest, and the principal payments due will be cut by fifty per cent.
What will be the effect on the 138 men who paid in full and the 161 who paid in part? I know they have no legal claim; but human nature being what it is, it would be too much to expect that some of these men would not say, either to themselves or openly, that they had made a mistake; that they should not have made those payments, and that those

Soldier Settlement Act
who did make them were not faring any better than those who did not. Those who had made no payments were faring no worse because they had not made them. They were not disturbed on their land.
The last day the subject was before the house, and again to-day the minister told us that the convention of the legion at Fort William had not asked for anything more than what is contained in the legislation. That is true. I hold in my hand a copy of a resolution adopted at the seventh dominion convention of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League at Fort William in January, 1938. Under the heading of soldier settlement, it states:
This convention realizing that among soldier settlers as a group there are a proportion who are in an exceedingly unhappy position in relation to their financial obligations to the board, urges the government to develop a policy which will enable them to continue to earn a livelihood on their farms notwithstanding the position of their accounts.
This convention further realizes that there are a number of soldier settlers to whom the dollar for dollar bonus has been of little assistance owing to adverse crop conditions and we would urge that this concessoin should be continued to this group or that some other means should be devised to afford them relief in lieu thereof.
' The minister was perfectly right in what he said, but I do not think that resolution passed at Fort William was fair to those who in that same district had made their payments regardless of crop failure or adverse crop conditions, the term used in the resolution. These men are going to be shut out from the benefits from now on. Another suggestion was made, as follows:
Information made available indicates that many soldier settlers have secured a large measure of relief as a result of taking advantage of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and the convention suggests that all soldier settlers should carefully examine the provisions of this act and take full advantage thereof.
At the time that suggestion was made I do not think there was any knowledge of the fact that legislation was going to be introduced in this house providing for the termination of those benefits at some date to be set in the future. If this suggestion is followed, knowing human nature as we do, we know that some men will say to themselves, "They are not going to give us any assistance by way of a fifty-fifty bonus; we cannot come under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act as we are not insolvent; we do not want to go through bankruptcy; the thing to do is to refrain from making any further payments; we will use our money for other purposes and then when we become
51952-SO	REVISED
eligible for the bankruptcy court we can follow the advice given here." I find that the suggestion to come under the provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act did not come only from that convention held in Fort William. I hold in my hand, "The report of the Department of Immigration and Colonization including report of soldier settlement of Canada for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1935," and on page 99 I find the following:
Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934
This act passed at the 1934 session of parliament is intended to provide a simple means whereby the debt burdens of the farmer may be adjusted to a level more consistent with the revenue producing capacity of the farm. The act makes provisions for farmers as debtors and their creditors to get together and arrange mutually satisfactory compromises and settlements.
The provisions of this act are applicable to debtors of the crown and therefore all classes of settlers under the department holding contracts with the director of soldier settlement are eligible to apply for the benefits of this legislation. The administative machinery began to function only in November, 1934, consequently it is too early to make any reliable estimate of the number of settlers likely to apply for reduction of their debt to the department or adjustment of the terms of existing contracts. To date 77 soldier settlers, ten British families and 83 civilian settlers have made application for reduction of debt or revision of terms of their contracts.
The report then goes on to deal with departmental cooperation with farmers' creditors act administration. The suggestion was made three years ago by the department that advantage should be taken of legislation which required that a man be insolvent before he could come under its terms. There is one other matter I should like to draw to the attention of the minister and the committee. I think it is to the credit of those who have spoken about the position of the soldier settler under the act, but we must not overlook the fact that to-day the majority of those concerned are not soldier settlers. I think if that fact were realized this matter would be looked upon differently. Even as early as three years ago only fifty per cent of the farms under the administrator were occupied by soldier settlers, and the percentage is less to-day. The report has this to say:
A total of 3,346 families came forward for settlement of which 183 withdrew from the scheme before receiving advances, and 1,335 withdrew after contracting loans, a total of 1,518 withdrawals. There are now 1,813 British families operating their farms under this scheme.	Fifteen settlers have repaid their
loans.
These lands either have been sold to civilian settlers or are still in the hands of the board.
EUmON
125S
Soldier Settlement Act

The net result is that a large percentage of the relief and benefits to be given under this legislation will go to civilian settlers who purchased land from the board prior to January 1, 1933. Those who purchased land in 1932 at the depth of the depression and did not pay anything upon it are now able to take advantage of this legislation and obtain a reduced interest rate of two and a half per cent and a reduction in payments of fifty per cent. I do not know what anyone can do about this now, but those are the facts. This scheme was initiated twenty years ago and to-day the number of soldier settlers is only a small percentage of the total, while the original soldier settlers represent even a smaller percentage. That being the case, I suggest to the minister that this should be treated as an ordinary collection matter. It really represents money which is outstanding to tiie government, some of it by civilian settlers who purchased these lands. These moneys have not been paid, and it is merely a matter of collecting them in the most efficient manner. We have a farm loan board which I believe is collecting all payments that it is possible to collect. It might be a good thing for the committee and the department and the minister to consider the advisability of placing the collection of these outstanding amounts under the farm loan board. I would not suggest this to the committee if the majority of these settlers were soldier settlers, but that is not the case to-day.

I deplore the suggestion that the dollar for dollar privilege be cut off at the present time. A few moments ago the minister said that the soldiers who had availed themselves of this settlement scheme were in a preferred position. In theory that may be so, but if the minister could see some of the farms in the district west of London upon which soldiers have been placed I do not think he would make that statement. I do not know why these farms were acquired by the board, but the fact is that they were. These lands will not produce and the soldiers who are still there are certainly not in any preferred position. They are fighting a little war of their own in order to keep body and soul together. My submission is that if this dollar for dollar bonus is cut off, we shall have more payments to make under the War Veterans' Allowance Act. In the end this will turn out to be poor economy. I urge the minister to continue this privilege until times are better.

I should like to refer to this question of the dollar for dollar bonus as there is a group of returned men in my constituency who are in desperate

need of real assistance. A moment ago the minister said that a soldier would not ask for anything that was unfair. I think that is correct, but I believe, if the minister were a little more familiar with the conditions under which some of these returned men live, he would be more lenient. I do not think the bill as it is now before us is as good as it was in its old form. Just at a time when these men need consideration, this dollar for dollar bonus is going to be cut off. It is a shame that such a step should be considered when these people need the bonus so badly. In order that the minister may have the exact words of some of these soldiers, I should like to read a resolution I received the other day. The following resolution was submitted to a meeting held on January 16, 1938, of soldier settlers on the Pope lease, and unanimously approved:
Whereas the dominion parliament at its session in 1933, by amendment to the Soldier Settlement Act, made provision for a bonus of a dollar for each dollar paid by or on account of each soldier settler; and
Whereas the said bonus terminates on March 1, 1938; and
Whereas owing to poor crops through hail damage and drought, together with low prices for agricultural products, the resident soldier settlers have been unable to take advantage of the bonus plan to any extent to date; and
Whereas we believe that it would be for the advantage of the dominion that soldier settler liabilities be liquidated at the soonest possible moment;
Therefore be it resolved that we the soldier settlers on the Pope lease ask the dominion government to seriously consider the advisability of continuing the bonus plan for a further period of five years;
That the maximum amount bonusable in any one year be the amount of the settler's indebtedness;
That interest, together with arrears of interest since 1929, be waived for a like period.
There is one point to which I particularly want to draw attention, and that is that this was a resolution from returned soldier settlers and was unanimously passed. I do not think they are asking for anything too much because they are in a very serious situation. They are in the drought area. I am not so much concerned about those who are in a position to pay because they were probably of a more speculative nature, have taken advantage of the dollar for dollar bonus, and have their land cleared of debt, but surely these other soldier settlers who offered their lives in the service of their country should receive a little consideration at this time. As I mentioned a few days ago when we were discussing this matter on the estimates, surely we should not deprive the soldier

Railway Act-Grain Rates
who may get a good crop next year and desires to clear off his indebtedness to the government, of the privilege of taking advantage of this dollar for dollar bonus, and getting his land clear as quickly as possible, but under the new bill he will not be permitted to take advantage of the bonus so far as new payments are concerned, because it applies only to arrears. While the extended period continues for only about two years-and of course that should be carried on-there is no good reason why it should not be continued even after the expiration of this bill. I think it would be in the interests of economy as suggested by the last speaker (Mr. Betts) that right now when people are so very hard up, especially these returned men, this dollar for dollar bonus should be continued and certainly not be cut off at this time.

May I ask the minister
whether, in the payment, of this bonus, the arrears or the current instalment must be paid first? In 1939, for example, would the soldier settler pay his arrears first, or would he have to pay the current instalment first, and then the arrears, and get credit for what he had paid?

If he has payments to make he can apply them on arrears of principal and interest and get the full advantage of the bonus. The worst that happens to him then is that he would be required to carry his 1939 payment, assuming that he could not meet it at five per cent interest.
If he has $100 to pay, he will pay that on the arrears, and get a credit bonus of $200?
Yes, a bonus of $100.
Provided he has paid taxes and insurance up to date. They come first. Is that not so?
Not necessarily.

I think the minister will find that that is how the scheme works out in practice, at all events. Before the man can get the dollar for dollar bonus he must have his taxes and insurance paid up to date.

I quite agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and others who have spoken on this bill, that conditions prevailing to-day are such that the government would be justified in continuing the same procedure we have had since 1933. The 1933 legislation was no doubt based on conditions at that time; its continuation was also based on the then prevailing conditions, and everyone who has sat in this house and 51592-80J
listened to statements made by the western members, particularly those who come from the drought areas, or heard the hon. member from Prince Edward Island describing conditions in his province, must realize the conditions that now prevail.
The hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas) has also mentioned that a number of soldier settlers in the St. John district had to give up their farms; and in New Brunswick, principally in the potato-producing area of the province, these men have not been able to receive satisfactory compensation for the potatoes they produced, selling them at twenty-five to thirty or forty cents a barrel, while the cost of production was twice as much. In justice to the returned soldiers and to others who have these farms, this bonus should be continued not merely as regards the arrears for the past few years but also to give these men an opportunity to pay off their indebtedness. I realize, as the minister has said, that this government has been generous, and past governments have been more than generous, to the returned soldiers in this matter; but these settlers are in a more or less hopeless condition, and the government may as well realize the situation now as later and give these men the benefit of the bonus so that they may be able to help themselves in the future.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OF CROWSNEST PASS RATES ON GRAIN WESTWARD AS WELL AS EASTWARD

speechtext:
Mr. THOMAS REID (New Westminster) moved the second reading of Bill No. 18, to amend the Railway Act (rates on grain).
He said:	Without going into any lengthy
explanation of this bill, I may say that, in brief, it asks that the same railway rates which apply on all grain and grain products from the three prairie provinces eastward to Fort William and eastern centres shall apply to all grain and grain products from those three provinces westward to British Columbia. Inasmuch as I have brought this matter up in the housv every year since 1930, perhaps it will not be necessary for me to go into it as extensively in every detail on this occasion. However, as there are many hon. members now present who were not here when similar bills were before the house on previous occasions, it might be
Railway Act-Grain Rates

advisable for me again to go over some of the main arguments in support of British Columbia's appeal for equal treatment with the middle and eastern provinces in the matter of railway rates on grain and grain products.
Briefly, the history of the matter is this. In 1897 legislation was enacted whereby the Canadian Pacific Railway agreed to construct a railway from Lethbridge, Alberta, to Nelson, British Columbia. For this they received a large subsidy in money and a grant of land. In return they were to reduce the then existing railway rates eastward by three cents per 100 pounds. These rates, from that time on, became known as the Crowsnest Pass rates. As my time is limited I cannot go into a detailed history, but I may point out that in general these rates placed upon the statute book in 1897 have been maintained ever since. In 1925, however, the matter was again brought before parliament, and new legislation was passed by the house in that year confirming the Crowsnest Pass rates as established in 1897, but extending them to apply on all Canadian National and Canadian Pacific lines. The Canadian Pacific Railway gained by this move as commodity rates were taken out of the freight list. The rates on grain and grain products were left as before but they applied only to points eastward, and British Columbia was again ignored. British Columbia has contended that the people of that province are entitled to the same treatment as the people in other parts of Canada, but that, on the contrary, she has been grossly and unjustly dealt with, as I shall show presently. The unjust treatment meted out to the people of that province constitutes a grievous burden. '
I am not going into a lengthy discussion of freight rates generally because I realize that this perhaps is not the place to do so; rather I shall confine my remarks to railway rates applying to grain and grain products eastward and westward. The House of Commons, having on previous occasions dealt with this very question, can and should, I submit, do so again. Before I discuss some of the injustices and anomalies of the situation, I wish to repeat what I have on previous occasions endeavoured to make clear, namely, that we have going into British Columbia the lowest grade of any railway line in any province. It appears that we from British Columbia have to repeat this statement over and over again because there are still some people who seem to think that, going through the coast range mountains to the Pacific, there are other grades to contend with. Not only have we the lowest grades but we have also the lowest upkeep expense on any portion of
'Mr. Reid.]
the trans-Canada railway-lower than in any other part of Canada. Construction costs were less and upkeep costs are lower than in other parts of Canada, as I shall show. In the sworn testimony given in 1925 before the board of railway commissioners information was given with reference to this matter. It was shown that the cost per mile of line between Kamloops and Hope, which is one of the heavy grades of railway going through British Columbia, was $133,563 per mile of 168 miles. From Montreal to Ottawa, a district all hon. members know fairly well, the distance is 111 miles and the cost was $178,614 per mile. Again, from Hope to Fraser Junction, a distance of seventy-seven miles, the cost was $51,544 per mile as against Joliette to Gamier Junction, a distance of 61-49 miles, which cost $62,394 per mile. As regards operating cost, I know that in the minds of many hon. members there is the idea that the grade through the mountains into British Columbia not only has cost more to construct but is also more costly to maintain. In the same testimony given at the time to which I have referred it was shown that the upkeep cost per mile in British Columbia was $3,825 per mile as against an upkeep cost in the prairies of $4,702 per mile.
One could take an entire evening giving data such as I have briefly touched upon, but I believe I have placed before the house enough to show that in the sworn testimony given before the board of railway commissioners it was made abundantly clear that in British Columbia construction costs were less, upkeep was less, and fewer double engines or, if I may so describe them, pusher engines are required than in certain parts of the prairies and of eastern Canada. There is no justification for a difference of between twenty and eighty per cent of increased railway rates in the west as compared with the east, and I am going to take time to quote a few of the different rates.
From Calgary to Vancouver the rate for export is twenty cents per 100 pounds over a distance of 642 miles, or 766 miles from Edmonton to Vancouver. Here I want the house to note the fact. While the Canadian Pacific railway is and has been taken as the yardstick by the board of railway commissioners, when it comes to computing the distance between the prairie province of Alberta and the province of British Columbia, they take the longer distance of the Canadian National, not the shorter distance of 642 miles, but 766 miles. They do not use the Canadian Pacific railway yardstick in that case. Of course it is to the advantage of the Canadian

Railway Act-Grain Rates
Pacific railway that the Canadian National mileage is quoted from Edmonton to Vancouver.

speechtext: Is it not the other way about? From Calgary to Vancouver is 642 miles.

subtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OF CROWSNEST PASS RATES ON GRAIN WESTWARD AS WELL AS EASTWARD
speechtext:
Yes, that is correct. The export rate is twenty cents per 100 pounds. At the moment a temporary rate has been put in, with which I shall deal later on, which allows certain varieties or grades of feed grain to be hauled at a rate of some 31 i cents; but mill feed, the greater part of which is used in feeding poultry and dairy stock, is still charged 411 cents, from either Edmonton or Calgary.
That is the rate westward on grain. Let us now see what the rate is going east. From Calgary to Fort William the distance is 1,242 miles. The grain rate for that haul is twenty-six cents. Strange to say, it is only when grain is going west that the railway companies differentiate between domestic and export rates. Grain leaving Calgary and Edmonton for Fort William and other points east is simply grain; in most instances there are no two rates. From Calgary to Montreal, a distance of 2,221 miles, the export rate is fifty cents, as against forty-six cents for domestic. From Calgary to Quebec, 2,215 miles, the rates are the same, fifty cents for export and forty-six cents for domestic.

subtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OF CROWSNEST PASS RATES ON GRAIN WESTWARD AS WELL AS EASTWARD
speechtext: Is it not the other way about, the cheaper rate for export?

subtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OF CROWSNEST PASS RATES ON GRAIN WESTWARD AS WELL AS EASTWARD
speechtext:
To some points in the east the domestic rate is lower than the export rate. From Fort William to Montreal, a distance of 995 miles, the rates quoted to me are twenty-four cents for export and only twenty cents for domestic. There were some exceptional rates put in there, and in some instances the domestic rate was really lower than the export rate, for reasons which I think will be explained by the minister. These figures were given to me by officials of the board of railway commissioners.
Now how does that work out? From Calgary to Vancouver the rate per ton per mile works out at -654 cents as against the rate from Calgary to Fort William of -418 cents. Or if you take the rate per 100 pounds per mile, from Calgary to Vancouver it is -0327 cents as against a rate from Calgary to Fort William of -0209 cents. The rate per ton per 100 miles-100 miles being the usual day's run of a train-is 65-4 cents from Calgary to Vancouver, and only 41-8 cents from Calgary to Fort William. The export rate to Vancouver as compared with that to Fort William is one-half cent more per mile. I mention that
because it is often said that the twenty cent rate, which is the export rate from Calgary and Edmonton to Vancouver, is equal to the rate from Calgary and Edmonton to Fort William. These figures which I have just given disprove that statement, showing that even on grain for export British Columbia does not enjoy the same rates as the east, let alone the domestic rate.
I now mention one or two other rates to show the difference between east and west. From Windsor, Ontario, to Saint John, New Brunswick, the distance is 1054-6 miles and the rate is 181 cents. If you were shipping the grain the same distance to Vancouver or New Westminster, the charge would be twenty-four cents. From Goderich, 962-6 miles, the rate is 181 cents, while westward the same distance, from a. place called Rusylvia, Alberta, 961-4 miles, the rate would be twenty-four cents.
One could take up considerable time placing before the house rates from various centres throughout Canada, but I think the few I have given amply demonstrate what I am endeavouring to bring out, that is that the rates westward are anything from twenty to eighty per cent higher than the rates eastward from Calgary and Edmonton. In passing may I point out that the railways seem to have a most idiotic rate structure, operating to the disadvantage of British Columbia. If one wants to ship butter or eggs from Vancouver or New Westminster to Calgary or Edmonton, a certain rate will be charged, but the farmer shipping similar goods from Edmonton or Calgary to New Westminster or Vancouver would have a cheaper rate. It is like charging a passenger so much for going in one direction, but charging him a different fare when he returned. I mention that to substantiate the argument I am making, that we in British Columbia are carrying an extremely heavy burden in the matter of freight rates. British Columbia is not asking for special treatment, and would any hon. member maintain that British Columbia should be forever discriminated against?
In arguing before the board of railway commissioners when counsel for both railway systems were present, I asked this question: Does the export rate on grain from the prairie provinces to British Columbia pay? No answer. Neither counsel would answer that question. I was hoping they would. If it does pay, why should they charge the people of British Columbia twice that rate for their domestic grain requirements? Again, if it does not pay, should the people of British Columbia be called upon to bear that load,
Railway Act-Grain Rates

while our competitors in countries like China, Japan and elsewhere receive good Canadian grain at half the freight cost at which we who live in British Columbia can get that same grain?
I now put to the house just what this means to the people of British Columbia. It is estimated by those who claim to know that five bushels of grain are consumed annually by the average individual, either in the form of flour-and including, of course, oatmeal too-or cereal. If we take the population of British Columbia at some 700,000 people, this means that they would consume 3,500,000 bushels of grain, equal to 160,000 tons, on which they are charged twice the rate paid on flour and grain going to New Westminster or Vancouver for export. This means that for many years past the people of our province have been paying 1415,000 more annually for their flour and grain requirements than the people in the eastern and central provinces have paid.
There is close to my own home one cooperative organization of which I have some knowledge. They have a membership of some six hundred persons, and they are out to buy for their members grain as cheaply as possible. Each year there is a dividend declared, so it cannot be said by the minister or anyone else that if freight rates were lowered the saving would not be passed on to the consumer, because in this cooperative organization they do pass on the profits to their members. Last year they purchased over five thousand tons of grain for their members. If the Vancouver basis had been in force on 5,0S3 tons at 204 cents per 100 pounds, they would have paid S20,840. Instead, on 3,646 tons they had to pay at the rate of thirty-one cents per 100 pounds, or a total of $22,969, and on 1,437 tons at the rate of 411 cents per 100 pounds, a total of $11,927, or a grand total of S34,896. egg-laying province in Canada, and on the average flock of five hundred birds this would mean a saving of $110 per year. I do not believe it is a fair comparison to compare even the rates in the United States

with those in Canada, because the freight structure or freight traffic in that country is entirely different from the freight structure or traffic conditions in Canada. In the first place, they have not the great grain trade that we have. They have more commodity goods. Then, the division of their passenger and freight traffic is entirely different.
It might interest hon. members to know that in the United States fourteen per cent of the revenue is from passengers; in Great Britain, thirty-seven per cent; in Germany, twenty-eight per cent; in Japan, sixty per cent and in Canada, twenty-four per cent. In an endeavour to prove that so far as grain is concerned rates in Canada to the west are not cheaper than the rate from central or eastern to western portions of the United States, let me give the following examples.
Cut Bank, in Montana, is 732 miles from Seattle. They have no export or domestic rate, as such, but operate only on one rate, and carry all grain for thirty-eight cents. In British Columbia we are charged 414 cents for mill feeds over a distance of 642 miles. Bozeman, another point in Montana, is 764 miles from Seattle and the rate is 384 cents. Billings, Montana, is 1,012 miles from Seattle, and the rate is 404 cents.
I ask the minister and the house to compare that with a rate of 414 cents for 642 miles from Calgary to New Westminster or Vancouver. Even if the rates in the United States are a little higher, they are hardly comparable when one takes into consideration the wages paid to the railway men across the line. The wages paid to railway workers in the United States average eighteen per cent more than those paid to Canadian workmen, while on the average the freight rates are only some seven per cent higher. As I have pointed out, it is hardly fair to compare a country like the United States with Canada because their freight structure and general traffic conditions are entirely different.

In the lower mainland of British Columbia a considerable area is set aside to fruit growing, and it is necessary that a considerable quantity of fresh fruit be exported in order that the industry may have sufficient returns to place it on a healthy basis. I should like to give one instance of discrimination in connection with railways and their tariffs, and more particularly under the express tariff. I understand that an Ontario fruit grower shipping berries from Grimsby, Ontario, to Montreal, Quebec, a distance of about 495 miles, has to pay only ninety-five cents per 100 pounds express. This afternoon a chairman of a committee when presenting his report referred to the freight rates on agricultural implements going west. The hon. member has been quite in order to-night in drawing these matters to the attention of those residing in eastern Canada. There is no doubt that these discriminations have hindered the development of many of the resources of our province. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have written off by statute large sums of money in connection with the purchase of lands now occupied by soldier settlers. That was done by the late government, and also by the government which preceded it; but it was regarded as very unsound business that we should continue to write off, by appropriations made by the Minister of Finance, vast sums of money in this way, and it was believed that a more urgent effort should be made to collect.
It was therefore determined to create an incentive to payment. It was believed that it would be a powerful lever in securing money if we undertook to credit a soldier with S2 for every $1 payment that he made. The effect of that was to get away from the necessity of making appropriations every year by the Minister of Finance based upon just crude estimates. On the other hand, it afforded an opportunity for those who so desired to make payments on the basis of their contract being about fifty per cent of the amount that was due under it. I plead with the minister to consider carefully the situation before he finally makes up his mind with respect to that. We extended until 1936 the time within which a payment of $1 would secure a credit of $2, and in 1936, since this government came into office, the time was further extended until March 31, 1938. At that time it was suggested that a little longer period should be granted for this benefit to continue for the soldier, but that view did not commend itself to the government at that time.

Yes, quite right. Someone in this chamber had suggested five years; but that was not acceptable to the government; as events proved, it was not acceptable to the senate, and the period was re-

Soldier Settlement Act
duced to two years. I suggest it would be well to extend the provisions of the section only for another period of three years; that is, from 1938 to 1941. I am not suggesting this with the idea that we are offering any great concessions so far as this country is concerned; but I firmly believe that if we do this we shall get some money, whereas if we do not do it, I am afraid we are going to be confronted with a situation that will compel us to make appropriations out of the consolidated revenue fund by writing down the value of the assets in connection with these lands that we have disposed of to soldier settlers. I am quite satisfied that if the minister will give the matter consideration from that angle, he will find on looking through the returns that if he does this and still offers credit of S2 for every SI paid until 1941, he will have given a reasonable opportunity for those who desire to pay to do so and will have created an incentive on the part of those who desire to retain their places and who feel that they can undertake a reasonable responsibility but will not undertake the responsibility of paying at the prices the contracts now bear.
1 can speak from personal discussion with many men who have had the benefit of this legislation, and I have been amazed at the zeal they have displayed securing money with which to make payment and thereby secure credit for twice the amount paid. I believe that we shall have done a good job for the Dominion of Canada and secured more money if we merely reenact the section as it appears, extending the period to 1941; or, if the minister feels that this is too long a period, I suggest that he might try it for, at any rate, a couple of years longer. I earnestly believe-and I say this entirely divested of any feeling in the matter except from my observations and inquiries-Ahat we shall haye secured more money at the end of 1940 if we make the period two years than we could possibly receive if we depended upon payments being made in the future on the basis of the present value of the contracts, except as the obligations may be reduced by reason of the provisions of the legislation now before the house with respect to past instalments. That is my conviction, and I should like the minister to consider the matter from that angle, because it was that consideration which induced the late government to initiate the legislation. If the minister will look at the records I think he will agree that the hope then entertained has not been wholly without tangible results. I know of nothing that makes one feel worse than to realize the amount of money we have lost in this transaction. It is attributable not so much to wrong judgment as to a feeling of optimism, with respect to productive values, which was not warranted by results. In the same way we lost vast sums of money in connection with another enterprise we entered into during and after the war. We lost in the aggregate, I think, some 380,000,000.
The losses we have sustained in connection with the soldier settlement lands can be attributed not so much to maldistribution, to recklessness or to carelessness, as to an estimate of productive value which subsequent events have not warranted. If, however, the result that I have indicated were found only in soldier settlement lands, it would be good cause for alleging negligence and lack of proper supervision and care. But every one of us, from western Canada in particular, knows that the hope of productive value, the belief in high prices for wheat and large production, was widespread. I can recall a minister telling us in western Canada that all we had to do was to go forward and produce half a billion bushels of wheat, because everybody believed that, as the result of the war, it would be a long time before the belligerent nations would be able to satisfy their own requirements, and we would always be able to supply their demands. We have always been able more than to supply their demands, and it was on that basis that this settlement took place, and that the high values I have mentioned were attached to lands. Of course, they could not be realized at the present time, and the result has been that very large sums have had to be wiped out as depreciation in values; and, finally, we have had recourse to the method which I have indicated.
If it is not going too far I would suggest to the minister that he might give this matter further study and consider whether or not it would be possible to make an extension for a further period of, say only two years. For I believe-once again I repeat it; I cannot stress it too strongly-speaking from observation and inquiry, that we shall receive more money at the end of two years by continuing this policy, giving credit of $2 for every SI paid, than if we adopt the method indicated by the bill, hoping to recover in full the balance of instalments in connection with the obligations incurred by settlers.
