Under the dollar for dollar bonus $1,409,000 has been collected.
Progress reported.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair.
Post offices, including salaries and other expenses of headquarters and staff post offices and supplies and equipment for revenue post offices, $14,624,470.

Would the minister give us a statement regarding any change in the number of post offices in Canada? I see by the annual report that there has been a decrease in Nova Scotia, and apparently there has been no increase in the Northwest Territories in spite of the developments going on there.

I cannot give the increases or decreases. I can give the total number by provinces:
Ontario	 2,618
Quebec	  2,578
Nova Scotia	 1,546
New Brunswick	 1,020
Prince Edward Island	 114
Manitoba	 796
Saskatchewan	 1,498
Alberta	 1,253
British Columbia	 925
Yukon	 18
Northwest Territories	 20
12,386
Why is there a decrease in the number of post offices in Nova Scotia?

I am not sure as to the
reason. It may be because there is rural mail delivery, or it may be diminution of business making it not worth while to keep the offices open.
Loss of population. *

The other night I referred to the method of sale of stamps in the larger post offices. I stated that the information I Lave is that the government itself does not undertake the sale of stamps in some of the large post offices. Is such the fact, and, if so, why are private people allowed to sell stamps in public buildings?

What my hon. friend states is the fact, the reason being that in many cases the system is cheaper; the commissions are less than the cost would be if some official of the Post Office Department sold the stamps. It has been the practice for many years. My

Supply-Post Office
hon. friend brought it to my attention the other day. I do not know that, as acting Postmaster General, I particularly like to announce any change of policy, but I would think it is a matter worthy of consideration. That is as far as I can go.

I am very glad to have this admission from the acting Postmaster General, because it seems to me most absurd that we should establish large post offices and have wickets for the sale of everything except stamps, and that when it comes to the sale of stamps we hand it over to some private individual, who probably is a partisan worker who gets the concession and in his private capacity goes into a public building and there sells stamps. I know that in some cases the government have to go to the private party to buy stamps, buying, say $1,000 worth of stamps through this private party. It seems so absurd to have an arrangement of that kind that 1 hope it will not be long before the acting Postmaster General will take action to stop something which, in my opinion, should never have started.

As far as Halifax is concerned -and I speak now of the Halifax post office separate and apart from other post offices in Nova Sco'tia-the post office was under a postmaster; they have now merged the duties of inspector and postmaster and the one man is both. From time immemorial the stamps have been sold in the post office in a cage provided by the government, both in the old post office and in the new one. The two ladies who are the stamp vendors there have been there for years. They have the confidence of everyone; they are not party workers; they are not ward heelers; they have never taken part in politics, and my hon. friend has gone far afield when he says that it is a political reward. I have been nearly twenty-five years in public life, and no person has been appointed, while I have been in provincial or federal polities, as a party worker or ward heeler to any such position. These two ladies have the confidence of everyone in Halifax. They get a commission on the stamps sold and they are well deserving of it. I shall see that they are kept there as long as we are in power, and I believe hon. gentlemen opposite would also see that they are kept there, because they take no part in politics and are perfectly honest.	.
How many new post offices are in course of erection at the present time?
My hon. friend means buildings?
Yes.
That is a matter for the Public Works department.
Are any recommendations made by the Post Office Department to the Public Works department for the erection of such buildings?

I am afraid I am not sufficiently familiar with that to answer definitely; but I would judge that where it is proposed to erect a public building there must be some request from the Post Office Department, and perhaps also other departments, such as customs, which are going to use the building.

In past years post offices have gone up without the consent of the Post Office Department. I say so advisedly because I happen to know of such a case. I am just wondering if there are any buildings which are now being constructed by the Public Works department for subsequent use as post offices and of which the Post Office Department may not be aware.
Not to my knowledge, and not to the knowledge of the officials who are here.

To come down to a concrete case, take the post office which is to be erected here in Ottawa. Are the post office officials consulted in the matter; do they have the final say on the size and capacity of the building, or is the matter entirely in the hands of the Department of Public Works?
The work is done on and with the advice of the Post Office Department.

Are any steps being taken to increase the business of the post office savings bank. I notice by the annual report of the department that there has been a decrease of about $167,000 in the amount on deposit, and it does seem to me some steps should be taken to increase the business.
A good deal of advertising is done to attract deposits, but I am informed that this really is a matter for the Department of Finance.
What rate of interest is paid?
Two per cent.

In the details which are given at page 167 of the estimates, I notice an item covering commissions to postmasters on savings bank business. That item has been reduced from $8,000 to $5,000. What is the reason for that?
Supply-Post Office
It varies according to the amount of the deposits. There were fewer deposits; therefore the commission was smaller.

Has the department under consideration the purchase of certain bank buildings in the western provinces to be used for postal purposes? I believe it has been the policy of the Post Office Department under all governments occasionally to buy a bank building, particularly in western Canada, that has been closed. In the west there are a number of towns where there were three or four banks, and of late years conditions have been such that there has not been sufficient business for them all. They have sort of sawed off with each other, one bank closing its branch in this town and another bank closing its branch in the next town, and as a result there are some pretty good buildings available for post office purposes. They could be easily adapted for use in that way, and I know of two or three buildings practically for sale in my constituency. I think some negotiations have been carried on, and I wondered if the minister could inform us whether he has advised the Department of Public Works to purchase those buildings.
Could the hon. gentleman tell me at what points these excellent buildings are located?
Sintaluta is one.

I have no knowledge with regard to that. I am told that this has been done; that buildings have been purchased, but again this is a matter for the Department of Public Works. As my hon. friend knows, the handling of real estate and buildings, the erection of buildings and all that sort of thing, is in the hands of the Department of Public Works.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that something more should be done in regard to the savings bank branch of the Post Office Department. I find in talking even with members of the house that some of them do not know that there is such a branch, carrying on business and paying interest at the rate of two per cent. I have also run across lawyers who did not know very much about this branch.
You are not surprised at that, are you?

They are supposed to be our learned friends. This summer I was talking with one lawyer, and I told him that I considered the post office savings bank one of the most convenient methods of financing while travelling. I told him that if he had a

deposit with the post office in his home town, he could go into the post office savings bank in any town and draw out up to $50 in a day. I believe that amount has now been increased to $100, but he did not even know there was such a thing in existence. As I say, it is a most convenient way to finance travel anywhere in Canada. There is no exchange required, and of course, since you do not give a cheque but have your book marked, you do not require a three-cent stamp. I feel that something should be done in the way of advertising this branch, and I am amazed to see such a reduction in the deposits this year What were the deposits, say five years ago? Has there been a continual reduction?
I am afraid we have not that information.
If it is a matter for the finance department, I would urge upon the minister that the two departments get together and see if something cannot be done along that line.

I may say that the Postmaster General himself has under consideration the possibility of making it somewhat easier to withdraw deposits and perhaps in other respects to model the post office savings bank after the facilities that are offered in Great Britain. I must admit that I am not familiar with the branch, but I am informed that the Postmaster General has some improvements in mind.
Do the deposits go into the consolidated revenue fund?
Yes; they go right into the consolidated revenue fund.

It seems to me that if this branch were advertised fully and, if necessary, if the rate were increased to 2i per cent, this would be a wonderful means of assisting in the financing of the dominion. It would also give encouragement to the average fellow with five, ten or a hundred dollars to deposit. It seems to me it would give a wonderful stimulus to the circulation of dollars in the dominion.

I am surprised to hear the hon. member for The Battlefords rising to-night to ask that some encouragement be given the banking institutions of this country. However, I am very glad to hear that he has some views which may be of some assistance to the acting minister. Is there any limit as to the maximum amount that a depositor may deposit in the post office savings bank?

The limit is $5,000.

Supply-Post Office
Has the acting minister any information as to the number who have reached that maximum in the post office savings branch?
No, I have not that information.

One of the few pleasures enjoyed by people in distant areas is that they can obtain books from various libraries in nearby cities. In the United States I believe there are cheap postal rates on books from public libraries. The Canadian department might very well take that point into consideration, and see if it is not possible to establish a special postal rate for books coming from public libraries, so that the people might be able to make greater use of such books. At the present time I believe the rate in the United States is three cents for the first pound, and one cent for each additional pound thereafter.
If these rates were made effective in Canada, I believe this would not in any way interfere with the revenues of the department. As a matter of fact those revenues undoubtedly would be increased because many people in the outlying areas would take advantage of lower postal rates. I am not prepared at this time to discuss the matter at length, but those are a few facts which come to my mind. I am sure, if the acting minister went into the matter carefully, he would find that a rate similar to that in the United States would be beneficial to everyone concerned. For the sake of the department and for the pleasure of many people, I would ask that he give serious consideration to the matter.

I suppose the hon. member knows there is already on the order paper a resolution dealing with the matter. I take it there will be a discussion on the point when the resolution is before the house, and as a result of that discussion some policy may be framed. Meantime the rate on books within a radius of twenty miles is five cents per pound, parcel post, a rate which does not seem excessive. However, it may be possible to make that rate lower. It is a matter of policy in the department.
The resolution is far down on the order paper, and there is a possibility it might not be discussed.
That is true.

I believe this is the proper time to bring the matter to the attention of the minister. Although the rate may be five cents per pound, I think we might very well adopt the rate of the United States, namely three cents for the first pound and
one cent for each additional pound. I am asking that the minister give the matter full consideration, particularly in view of the fact that it will bring in greater revenue, rather than decrease it. After all, the cheaper the rate is, the more people will be able to use it.
I am sure the hon. member would not guarantee that, but we shall be glad to give the matter consideration.

How much does the Post Office Department receive from the chartered banks in Alberta for the distribution of their pamphlets containing the speeches of Mr. Vernon Knowles. Those pamphlets were distributed through the post offices, and I should like to know how much they received for that service.
The rate is one cent for two ounces.
That is not my question. I want to know how much the department received for that service.
I cannot tell the hon. member, because I have not the information here.
It would not be done gratis, would it?
Certainly not.

I wonder
if we can get the information at some other time.

I fail to see why any one
would assume that the post office is carrying mail gratis.

He said "distribution"
by the post office.

It is performing a service.
I understand it is not done free.
But that is his point.
The answer is no.

Is there any evidence of
that?
The evidence is-
Or is it just a guess?
Just what the officials tell me.

That the post office
was paid for distributing those pamphlets- does the minister say that?

I do not even know the
pamphlets were distributed. I have no personal knowledge of it.

I have
evidence of the fact, because almost every office in Alberta distributed them. '
Supply-Post Office
I would have to have knowledge first whether such an act took place. I do not know. But if any service was rendered through the post office, it had to be paid for it.

That is the reason I was struck by the fact that the hon. member seems to be in error. I can take a thousand pamphlets to a post office, pay them a given sum and they distribute them. That has been done-it was at one time.
It is still so.

I believe what the hon.
member has in mind is that same form of distribution. As I gathered it, he left the impression that pamphlets had been distributed through the post offices, and he wanted to know what was received as payment by the Post Office Department for that distribution. There used to be such a provision in our law; I never say anything "is" now, because the department changes so from time to time that one does not know what might happen over night. But there was a time when I could take a thousand pamphlets to a post office; they would have a list, and they would distribute them to all the people, even though the pamphlets may not be addressed. In some instances they are addressed with the words "To the householder." That is called householder distribution, for which I know I have paid. It is that which I believe the hon. member for Bow River had in mind.

I am told any service of that sort is paid for. But I think the hon. member will realize that he could hardly expect me at this time to say how much was paid for a certain service at a certain post office in western Canada, or anywhere else. At any rate, I have not that information.

I am not
pressing the question at this time, but I should like to know how much the Post Office Department received for that service. If the postmaster himself received it, would it be recorded in the books which were sent on to the department? There should be some record of it in the Post Office Department.

I am told there are about
30,000,000 pounds of that carried in a year. I am not sure that it would be worth while to have detailed information in the department on the point. At any rate, we have not the information, and I am inclined to think it is not worth while to keep a record of those services.
Then, the charge is left to the decision of the local postmaster, is it?
No; the local postmaster is not asked to keep that record.
There surely must be a standard charge for such service; it is very common.
For printed matter the rate is one cent for two ounces.
Does that include the cost of distribution as well?
That is the standard cost for distributing them.
The total cost to the party who mails them?
The total cost to the person who gets the service.

There are no stamps put on them, and I believe the hon. member concludes that it is a free distribution by the postmaster, as an individual, whereas, as a matter of fact I remember that a charge was levelled once that this was an interference with the postal laws of the country. For instance, you pay a fee; they distribute the material, and that is all there is to it. That goes on continually. I first learned about it by actual experience, and I found out that that was the way it was done. The postmaster himself gets nothing for it, except possible commissions on the receipts of his office.
Could the minister give us the number of depositors in the post office savings bank in the last year?

There are 49,551 accounts. There were 6,233 new accounts opened during the year, and 4,854 accounts closed. The number of accounts open at the end of the year stood at 80,370, or an increase of 1,379. When I said the total number of accounts was 49.551, I should have said that that was the number of deposits.
What was the total amount?
I believe it is more than that.
That is for the year. There is on deposit now a total of $21,879,593.13, a slight decrease.

What main factors are taken into consideration by the department in deciding whether a postal delivery service shall be established in certain centres?

Supply-Post Office
The chief factors are the revenue of the office and the population of the town.
It used to be 10,000 people.
What is the lowest population where a postal delivery service is in effect?

What place has pull
enough to make the arrangement without the necessary population?

I am afraid I cannot give the name of the town with the lowest population or revenue. I would have to repeat that the population is supposed to be at least 10,000 and the revenue about 835,000, but that may vary. The population may be higher and the revenue may be a little lower, or the revenue may be unusually high and the population less. That is left to the discretion of the department.
And the question of pull.
It may have been that way in the old days.
It was prior to 1930 and has been since.
I imagine there is not much use in the pot calling the kettle black. I dare say that under both administrations there was a little latitude in these matters.
There were so few left by 1930 that we had not a chance.

I am interested in knowing to what extent the concentration of population and the lay-out of the community would influence the department in arriving at a conclusion as to inaugurating a postal delivery service.
It may have a bearing, but I have no information.
Could the minister give us the dismissals of postmasters in 1936 and 1937 in the different provinces, and the reasons?

I have them for the last two years and for certain other two years. The figures I shall give now are for the last twenty-eight months, the period of the present administration:
Prince Edward Island	 3
Nova Scotia	 12
New Brunswick	 17
Quebec	 133
Ontario	 6
Manitoba	
Saskatchewan	 6

I may say that in the corresponding period the dismissals were as follows-
Who asked for that?
I am just giving it.
This will help to get your estimates through.
I am rather enjoying it.
This will help you to get them through.
I was wondering whether the asking of that question was intended to help me.
That used to be a commonplace question when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power.
I am not objecting.
Certainly not; that is your job, but you should hardly volunteer information.

I do not require any advice from my right hon. friend on that point. I shall discharge my duty as well as I can. I am not particularly familiar with this department, and if my right hon. friend is hinting that he is going to make it more difficult, it makes no difference to me whatsoever.
Mr. BEN'NETT: The minister was asked a civil question to which he replied, and then he started to give information which was not asked for with respect to a previous administration. He thinks that is going to help him get his estimates through. If an hon. member asks a question, the minister should give an answer, but he should not volunteer information which may have a political bearing.
That is exactly the reason the question was asked..
It was not.
I ask the minister to give us the information for the same period previously.
I asked the question simply for information.
I ask for the same information for the previous period.
I am sorry I began to give that information, and if my right hon. friend thinks it would promote the work of the committee; I am quite willing to omit giving it.

It was volunteered, but now it has been asked for.

Supply-Post Office

I shall not volunteer it now, I shall give it according to the request that is made for information during the previous administration. The figures are:
Prince Edward Island	 2
Nova Scotia	 68
New Brunswick	 26
Quebec	 35
Ontario	 7
Manitoba	 4
Saskatchewan	 1
Alberta	 1
British Columbia
I may say that in every case an investigation was held by a properly authorized commissioner. I should like to know what the twenty-eight month period covers, from what date to what date?

I shall have to add to the information that I gave. The dismissals I gave were those made on the personal statement of a member of parliament or on a postmaster's admission. Then there are those that followed as a result of investigation.
What dates are they?

Under the present administration the dismissals after investigation were as follows:
Prince Edward Island	
Nova Scotia	 7
New Brunswick	 11
Quebec	 107
Ontario	 3
Manitoba	
Saskatchewan	 1
Alberta	 4
British Columbia	
That is the information for the last twenty-eight months under the present administration.
Those are on investigation, and then there would be the dismissals on the say-so of a member.
I gave those.
The two together would give the total number of dismissals.
It would be 179 plus 133.
Did the minister say just three in Ontario?
Yes.
I want to compliment the Liberal members from Ontario for not being hard-boiled Grits.
Where a member protests against the postmaster having been partisan in an election, what proof must be submitted before action is taken?
You mean before an investigation is undertaken?
An investigation concerning the dismissal of a postmaster.

I think the Minister of Agriculture outlined the practice the other day. If a member states over his own signature that he has personal knowledge that a civil servant or a servant of the government has been partisan at an election, that is sufficient under an order in council to ensure his dismissal almost automatically. If anyone else makes a complaint, a commissioner is appointed, and if the minister regards his report as being sufficient to warrant a dismissal, the postmaster is dismissed.

It was that very answer which the Minister of Agriculture made in this chamber the other day which prompted me to ask that question. Personally I am not satisfied that any member of this house should exercise the prerogative of having an individual dismissed from the public service merely on the word of the member that to his knowledge the individual has been guilty of partisanship. If any member of this house, or an elected representative before he takes his seat, has knowledge that a person has been guilty of partisanship during an election, I think an investigation should be held anyhow, even though it be a member who makes the complaint. I know the acting Postmaster General is himself in a general way opposed to patronage, and I submit to him that, in all fairness, the individual accused of partisanship should be given an opportunity to submit his case to some body designated to investigate charges of that kind. The hon. member for Vancouver North the other day said that all that appeared in a communication upon which a certain person was dismissed from the public service was the statement that he had been guilty of participating in an election, and merely on a bald statement like that the man was dismissed. I do not think any hon. member will claim that that is fair to the individual concerned or that it is a good thing for the government of the country. If a member, I do not care who he may be, makes a statement charging a person with an offence, I think the least we can do is to ensure that the individual will be given an opportunity of replying to the charge. If justification be found for the charge that there has been participation in an election, then there could be little objection to dismissal after investigation; but I know of many members of parliament who, in their zeal to obtain a little patronage, might perhaps be a little more partisan in their activities than even postmasters during an election.

Supply-Post Office
I am not sure that I have any particular fault to find with that; but the practice has obtained, and I am quite sure that an order in council was passed.
In the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden.
Does the minister not think it is time the practice was changed?

Possibly so; but so long as that order in council is in force, I suppose the departments concerned will carry out its terms. Before I sit down I might add that in the Post Office Department, in every case where the revenue of the post office is $400 or more, whether or not the member states over his own signature that he has personal knowledge of the conduct of the official, an investigation is made.
Is that $400 a year or a month?
A year.
Is the accused given an opportunity of staling his case?
In the Post Office Department, yes, if the revenue is over $400 a year.
How many were dismissed by the former administration for political partisanship?
In Prince Edward Island, 5; Nova Scotia, 45; New Brunswick, 48; Quebec, 246; Ontario, 3; Manitoba, 6; Saskatchewan, 10; Alberta, none; British Columbia, none; a total of 363.
Does that cover a period of five years?
No; twenty-eight months.

Which twenty-eight
months, the first or the last?

The minister mentioned that during the last twenty months there had been only one dismissal in Alberta; but I have personal knowledge of three postmasters having been dismissed, and I can give the names of the places: Acme, Newcastle and Falher. They were all dismissed for alleged political partisanship, and yet the minister tells us there was only one dismissed. I cannot understand that.
During the period mentioned there was only one dismissed on the personal statement of the member, and four were dismissed after investigation.
Five altogether?
Five altogether.

I should like to bring
to the attention of the minister a matter of special importance, and one that is a little out of the ordinary course of departmental details. I assume the minister knows that there is in course of construction in the county of Leeds an international bridge. It is called the Ivy Lea bridge. It is unique in its character and because it is I wish to take about five minutes of the time of this committee in explaining its character.
The total length of the crossing from the Canadian side to the United States side is between six and eight miles. By far the greater portion of this distance is roadway, highways constructed on large and small islands. There are, as a matter of fact, only two spans of any substantial length, one in the United States channel and one in the Canadian channel, the intervening distance being occupied with islands and narrow crossings over narrow channels. This bridge passes through the whole of the Thousand Islands, and I have before me a statement that I am sure will surprise the committee when I say that it is issued over the signature of the advisory engineer of the Thousand Islands bridge authority. He says:
Within one day's drive or three hundred miles radius, there is located one-tliird of the population of Canada, and one-fourth of the population of the United States.
Note that, Mr. Chairman: Within three hundred miles of the end of this bridge this large proportion of the two populations is located, including New York and all the eastern states, Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa and other larger centres of population.
This bridge is to be formally opened, I think, in the month of August next, and the idea I have in mind in bringing this matter to the attention of the acting Postmaster General is to suggest that he consider the issuing of a special stamp to commemorate the event. Similar action is being advocated at Washington, and I believe is being favourably considered.
In addition, the possibilities of the development of tourist traffic, in which we are all interested, and which brings in an enormous amount of revenue to this country, are practically unlimited with a unique feature such as this, and they are being carefully studied by those interested in the matter. It has been brought to the attention of the tourist bureau, the Department of Mines and Resources and the Department of Transport. That is the suggestion I wish to make.
It is said that on a clear day one can see for sixteen miles up or down the St. Lawrence river from the United States main span, and
Supply-Post Office

fourteen miles from the Canadian span, and that view is just studded with islands. I do not need to tell the members of this committee that the Thousand Islands in the St. Lawrence constitute one of the great scenic features of the world, and this bridge traversing about eight miles through the heart of these islands is really something unique. I think it is worthy of consideration by the minister, whether it would not be to the advantage of the department from the standpoint of revenue, as well as advertisement in connection with tourist traffic, that a special stamp be issued to commemorate the opening of this bridge. I do not know whether any very large amount of cost is involved; but there will be a tremendous sale of post cards and all that sort of thing, and I think it would help to stimulate and promote the tourist traffic and at the same time bring in some additional revenue to the department. All I shall do is to ask the minister to consider the suggestion, investigate to find out what is being done in the United States and, if possible, lend the assistance of his department to the advertising of this attraction, in the hope that tourist traffic will be stimulated and developed and that this can be done to the advantage of Canada and without any immediate loss of revenue in connection with the issue of this stamp.

The general practice, I believe, is not to issue stamps except to commemorate something of great national importance. I do not say that this is not of that type and I shall be glad to give it consideration.

They are considering it in the United States. It is suggested that the Prime Minister of Canada and President Roosevelt should shake hands on this international bridge. I should be glad myself to have the minister come; I would shake hands with him.
That is quite an inducement.

Apparently there are about 12,000 post offices in Canada, but only about one-tenth of that number are empowered to transact post office savings bank business. Will the minister explain the basis on which that privilege is given to a post office? During the last two years many of the chartered banks have been closed in the smaller towns. Would it not be helpful to the citizens in such places if the right to deposit with the post office savings bank were made available to them?

I cannot say that there is any definite rule. Sometimes it is according to the

demand in the locality and the probabilities of there being substantial deposits to make it worth while. I cannot give any other answer. I believe that these branches are conducted in those post offices where money orders are issued.
Is it a fact then, that only one-tenth of the post offices in Canada can issue money orders? Surely that is not right.
No, that is not the case, nor is the reverse the case.

What was the total amount
of mail, in pounds or tons, carried last year?

First-class mail, 17,888.243 pounds; second-class, 121,575,000 pounds; third-class, 29,649.779 pounds; parcel post, 68.494,364 pounds. These checkups are taken only every few years. This is for last year. The plans are now being made for another enumeration this year.
Can the minister give the same information for the year before that?
No, I have not that.
Could that be looked up?
The enumeration is not made every year.
Could it be looked up for the committee before these estimates are completed?
I am informed that there is no information which can be given with regard to the poundage of the previous year. I am sorry, but we do not have it.

I wish to bring to the
attention of the acting minister something in connection with the appointment of a postmaster for the Beaverton post office. I shall not find fault with what the department has done, nor am I going to find fault with the civil service commission; for, having looked into both sides of the matter, I am satisfied that perhaps what was done was all that could have been done under the circumstances. These are the facts. Apparently according to custom, the vacancy in the post office was advertised, the postmaster having died, I believe. Six returned soldiers applied to take the examination, and, of course, the acting postmaster also made application. The acting postmaster having been there fifteen years, and apparently having been very well thought of in the village, he easily obtained better marks than the six returned soldiers, who had not the same experience. I looked into the particulars and found that they were different from what

Supply-Post Office
I had been told, and, as I have said, I now believe that what was done was probably all that could have been done. But I felt that in a similar case in the future, if the department knows, as it probably will know, that an acting postmaster has been filling a position for fifteen years in the post office and has a good reputation in the village, the department should not place returned soldiers in the position of being defeated, so to speak. They should not be put in a position where they will certainly not have a chance to obtain the post after taking the examination. If the department was satisfied that this acting postmaster was the one who should logically fill the job, he should have been given the job and these returned soldiers should not have been embarrassed in the way they W'ere and made to suffer defeat.

My hon. friend knows that
appointments of that kind are entirely within the purview of the civil service commission.

I realize that and I
am not finding fault with either the civil service commission or the department. What I am urging upon the acting minister is that if a similar case should arise in the future, and it is believed that the acting postmaster should be given the job, he should be given it without humiliating returned men.

I am inclined to believe
that under the law they must conduct examinations. I doubt whether the civil service commission would have the power to appoint an acting postmaster.

He cannot be promoted
under the regulations as they now are; he has to take his chance with others.

In this case they are not
civil servants and therefore the principle of promotion is not involved.

Would it be possible in such a case for a person who had not been in the Post Office Department at all to come in and pass the examination with the result that the man who had been in the position for a number of years would not receive promotion?

It is possible, except for the fact, of course, that the returned soldier always gets the preference; otherwise it is within the power of the commission to appoint whom they please, and they would appoint according to the rank which the applicant took in his examination. It might work an injustice, of course.

What struck me is that it seems hardly reasonable to examine these returned soldiers in a contest with a man who had already been acting postmaster and with fifteen years' experience. I am not finding any fault, but I feel sorry for the returned soldiers being up against an examination like that. If, as the leader of the opposition has said, the matter is purely in the hands of the civil service commission, I suppose nothing else could have been done.

There is a point I should like to clear up concerning the protection of mail matter. I am sure the acting Postmaster General will hasten to assure me that once a letter is mailed with a three-cent stamp on it, the department is prepared to use all the force at its command to see that that letter is not tampered with and is properly delivered. In fact it is a serious matter to tamper with: the royal mail. Then there comes to my mind the question of distribution of pamphlets at a rate of two cents an ounce, which I believe was quoted. If the minister is sure that the department will do everything in its power to protect mail, I should like him to give me some assurance. He must be aware that at the present time there is in effect in the province of Quebec a law known as the padlock law. If I intend to mail what I consider communistic propaganda in Quebec, is the acting Postmaster General in a position to tell me that he will rigorously protect my mail anu complete the transaction by effecting delivery of the pamphlets no matter what may be said by any provincial law? I think the acting Postmaster General should make that clear. If I go to the trouble of paying the postage on this mail, does the minister intend to protect my property while it is in the hands of the government and to assure me that it will reach its destination in the province of Quebec, since that is a part of Canada as well as any other part of the country, notwithstanding any law passed by that legislature?

All mail on which postage has been properly paid has the protection of the law. Indeed, I am informed that the safeguarding and inspection of the mails cost the department a million dollars a year. All mail on which postage is properly paid will be protected by the department and delivered. If it is communistic literature such as my hon. friend refers to, I should think it would be subject to the laws of the country; if it is subversive of the law and advocates violence or anything of that sort, I think it might very properly be shut out of the mails. Otherwise I see no reason why it should not be carried.
Supply-Post Office

Of course that depends on what interpretation is placed upon the term " communism." It is commonly known that there is in Quebec at the present time this so-called padlock law, and that under various pretexts certain homes have been entered and books seized. But I want the acting Postmaster General to assure me whether, no matter what sort of literature it is, as long as it does not come into conflict with dominion law, the Post Office Department is prepared to fight to the last degree to assure me that my mail will be delivered in Quebec, no matter what interpretation the Quebec government may place upon it.

I can give my hon. friend that assurance very readily. If the mail matter does not violate a law of the Dominion of Canada, as far as I am concerned the mail will be carried. I am not supposed to have any particular knowledge of the laws of Quebec, and in any case I do not think the laws of Quebec override those of the Dominion of Canada.
There has been a great deal of seizure of papers in the province of Quebec the moment they entered certain stations.
Not in the mails.
I am wondering whether that literature seized went by the mails or by other means of transportation.
None was seized in the mails.

I think the minister is in error as to that. The other day in the course of the discussion I directed attention to the fact that mail bags had actually been seized, and photographs of the mail bags were published in the press. My objection was to any provincial authority, because of an alleged breach of a provincial law, seizing a mail bag from the custody of those who had it under their control. The question arose in the United States on one occasion, as the minister will recall, and I was greatly concerned about this matter. However, I do not think the minister should answer this; it is a matter which the Minister of Justice should deal with, and, frankly, I do not think it is fair to ask the acting Postmaster General to answer the question. But I should like to know whether or not the statement and the photographs published in the press correctly represent the incident. That, I think, comes under his department. The legal inferences and conclusions to be drawn from the seizure are matters that can be dealt with by those whose duty it is. The minister can only give me information as to whether or not any mail bag was actually seized and taken out of the custody

and control of those who had it because it was alleged to contain communistic literature, and whether or not- that mail bag was held by those who alleged that it contained these papers and letters which it was said were being carried in breach of a provincial statute.

I have some knowledge of the incident to which my right hon. friend refers. There were certain photographs published in which mail bags were shown. It is quite true that the department supplied to the publishers of that paper, as it does to other publishers, mail bags for their convenience. But the contents do not become mail until they reach the post office, and although no doubt there were papers in these bags which were photographed, it was really not mail because it had not yet been delivered to the post office. The mail bags have been recovered.
How did it get into the mail bags if it was not mail?
It is not mail until the postage has been paid on it.
Where were those particular bags sent from?
The bags were, I understand, delivered to the publishing house.
Where?
I think in Ontario, and the mail carried to Quebec. That is my difficulty.

I am not sure about that; but the point I want to make is that all these publishing houses, for the convenience of the publishers and, I suppose, of the Post Office Department, have empty mail bags delivered to them, and these are filled with the publication and taken to the post office, but it is not mail until it is actually in the post office. These were the bags that were seized and photographed.
I do not want to press the point unduly because I do not think the minister is in a position to answer the legal question involved-
No, I would not attempt that.

-but I think he has overlooked one fact. The information published in the press indicated that the mail bags furnished by the department for the carriage of the papers were furnished in Ontario, and the papers having been placed in the bags, the bags were placed in a railway mail car and

Supply-Post Office
transported to the province of Quebec. When they went into the mail car they went into his majesty's mail.
I would think so.

I think that is clear. And they were delivered at a railway station in Montreal and, under the alleged authority of a provincial statute, were seized before they could be taken to the post office for distribution. That is the story, as I gather it from the press. The photograph of the mail bags was published in the press. Now the issue is a narrow one; it is whether or not there is any authority to interfere with his majesty's mails on the part of those who allege a breach of a provincial statute, when the bags are in the custody and under the control of the Post Office Department; for those bags being carried in the mail car I am informed were under the control of the Post Office Department. They have vans which carry them on to the post office. In the first instance it gets down to a question of essential fact. I can only say that I am not informed as to that, beyond what I saw in the newspaper. I did mention it to the Minister of Justice the other day, and I think the matter is so serious that we should have some clear understanding as to just what are the circumstances.

I am afraid I have not all the information that perhaps I should have. Apparently I was mistaken when I said that these bags did not come from Toronto or Ontario. I understand now that they did. This representation is made to me, however, that those bags contained mail, technically mail, while they were in the baggage car or the mail car, whichever it was, which carried the mail into Quebec, but that they were then delivered into the custody of a publishing house in that province, which completed the work of the Post Office Department.
Yes; their transit was over.
After that they were no longer in the custody of the Post Office Department. As to the legal aspect of the matter I am not going to express an opinion.
The point I made previously was that literature of that kind had been seized at the railway station.
That was what I saw in the press, that one seizure was made at the station, before the bags had been taken to the publishing house.
I have no information on that at all, nor have the officials.

I have given the answer already; my hon. friend asked exactly the same question previously, and I answered it. I do not suppose I need answer it again. I may say this to my hon. friend, however, that he is quite right when he says that once mail bags are placed in a car which carries his majesty's seal, no one can interfere with those bags; but I understand that was not done. That mail was delivered out of that car into the headquarters of this publication in the province of Quebec, and then the work of the Post Office Department was completed. In any event that is the information I have. If my hon. friend has any information that a mail car was entered, I can only say that I have no knowledge as to that.
Or that the bags were seized at the station, which is what the newspapers said.
Not according to the information I have.

If there is even a thought that possibly the mails of Canada are being interfered with, it might be serious enough for the department to take some action in this regard, and inquire into the matter as fully as possible. If, for example, anyone attempted to even get near a car with the idea of seizing mail or for any other purpose, I feel sure the department would do everything within its power to see that the Canadian mail, or his majesty's mail, was fully protected. I feel that in this instance the matter is sufficiently serious for the department to take
Supply-Post Office

cognizance of it and fully inquire into all the circumstances in order to ascertain the exact position of the bags when they were seized.

I think the minister could easily say that he will give that assurance, because I think we are all interested in the matter, in order to ascertain what are the facts so that the minister may be able to state with authority just what has taken place in connection with the interference with these mail bags, whether they were then mail or not; whether they were in the custody of the crown, which is the Post Office Department, or whether the transit had ended. Certainly I feel that we should have those facts before us. I would, however, hardly expect the minister to have the details before him at the moment.
There is one other matter that I think the hon. member for Peace River should keep in mind. It is this: There is a right to interfere with his letter carrying the three-cent stamp if it contains lottery tickets, for instance, or matters of that sort. But that is not a provincial matter; that is power which is vested in the Post Office Department itself under the statute; for there is a certain amount of forbidden material in connection with which the department can exercise its jurisdiction.
But through the federal officers.

Yes. There are certain matters in regard to patent medicines, lottery tickets and so on; but the right of a provincial official or constable to allege that a mail bag contains something he does not like, and to take that mail bag out of the custody of the crown and impound it is something that, I believe, has been contested and fought against with great tenacity, and I tlhink it should continue to be fought against. But, as the minister has said, everything depends upon the facts.
Quite so, and they should be ascertained.

I think there is with regard to this matter a report which I shall certainly examine, but I am assured that this mail matter was not legally in the possession of the Post Office Department at the time the seizure was made. However, I shall make further investigation, and if the opportunity offers I may be able to give more complete details.

As far as I know there was more than one seizure made of papers and so on. I do not know whether they went 
through the mail or by express; but now that the minister has been made aware of the situation, I trust he will make his inquiries as complete as possible in order to ascertain all the facts in the matter.
Could the minister explain the machinery for apprehending forbidden mail such as that mentioned by the right hon. leader of the opposition, lottery tickets and material of that type?

I am going to read my hon. friend the section of the act bearing on that point. I would not be too confident that I could describe to -ham in detail the machinery which is set in operation, because really I am not very familiar with if. But the act states:
The Postmaster General may, subject to the provisions of this act-
(d) make regulations declaring what shall and what shall not be deemed to be mailable matter for the purposes of this act, and for restricting within reasonable limits the weight and dimensions of letters and packets and other articles sent by post, and for prohibiting and preventing the sending of explosive, dangerous, contraband or improper articles, obscene or immoral publications, prints or photographs, or obscene or immoral postcards, or letters or postcards having printed, stamped or written on the outside thereof any words or devices which, in the opinion of the postmaster general, tend to injuriously affect the commercial or social standing of the persons to whom they are addressed

I am not in a position to state exactly the procedure followed by the Post Office Department.
The Postmaster General is given power to make regulations governing various matters. What are the regulations now in force along these lines?

The Postal Guide, I believe, has a great many of them. There are literally hundreds, and I suppose my hon. friend might obtain a copy of that publication and examine them for himself. I do not suppose I could give them all to-night, and in any case I do not have them here. Is there any particular regulation on any particular subject on which my hon. friend desires information?
The particular point in which I am interested is to know where the duty is imposed? Do the regulations impose a duty on every postmaster and on every sub-postmaster, or whoever has charge?

The postmaster is instructed that when the appearance of anything in the mail leads him to believe that it contravenes the law, he must send it either to the dead letter office or to the inspector for the district who, in turn, sends it to Ottawa.

I do not desire to delay the committee; but in considering this question erf saving banks I have formed a very strong opinion, and I made up my mind some time ago that I would express it. The truth is that we have had only 820,000,000 odd in the postal savings banks of the country for a number of years. In New Zealand the Post Office Department maintains the following services: First, the post office; second, the long distance telephone; third, telegraph services in any fairly large community, and, fourth, the savings banks. The manager of the New Zealand postal service, Mr. McNamara, deals with this whole service as a matter of business. No interest is allowed on money taken in during the broken part of the month; that is, the interest does not begin to run until the first day of the succeeding month. No interest is paid upon broken sums of money; that is, the interest is paid only on even amounts. This money is loaned to the treasury of the Dominion of New Zealand, which pays interest upon it. The result was that in one year a substantial amount of money was earned, and there were loaned to the government very substantial sums of money which proved quite useful.
In Canada the delay in getting money out of the savings 'banks is so great that they have, I am sorry to say, [DOT] served no useful purpose. I realize it is quite unfair to direct these observations to the acting Postmaster General-we all regret the illness of the Postmaster General-but I want to put on record the suggestion that we should do something to increase our postal savings facilities. The need for these facilities is growing greater, in western Canada especially, as the chartered banks can no longer maintain many of their offices in the small communities, especially since these distressing days have arisen. The post office would always be in a position to receive deposits as they do in New Zealand and permit them to be withdrawn easily and quickly up to a certain amount. They have done something in this direction up to $50, but in practice there are apparently undue delays and it occurs to me that possibly something might be done to provide additional banking facilities, if I might use that term, for the population that has been denied the services of the chartered banks.

Supply-Post Office
The present rate of interest is two per cent, and with all deference I suggest that if we want to do the right thing we should pay at least two and a half per cent to these depositors. That is the way in which it occurs to me. I believe if these facilities were increased, this would prove conducive to thrift in communities where thrift is desirable and where such facilities are no longer available. That is my conviction with respect to the matter, and I thought I would bring it to the attention of the department.
I was impressed when one day I stopped in a remote community in New Zealand to have lunch, went into the post office and found that the postmaster was a trained telegrapher. He also had long distance telephone facilities, the post office and the savings bank. All these conveniences were under the one roof. When I came back to Wellington I saw Mr. McNamara who operates the whole postal service as an enterprise under his immediate control. I found that the sums of money that he was able to lend to the dominion were very large. A useful purpose was being served in New Zealand, and I do not think we have extended these facilities in Canada to the extent we should. I think we could strengthen our position considerably, just as has been done in Great Britain, where the postal savings amount to substantial sums of money and where the savings certificates also bring in large sums.
Then in the United States, a very rich country, we find the treasury in Washington providing facilities throughout the country for the purchase of certificates paying rates of interest higher than two per cent and maturing at the end of five or ten years, as the case may be. These certificates are sold in multiples up to 810,000, but I do not think we could go as far as that. However, this might be a matter for consideration by the Minister of Finance.
I do not suggest that the acting minister is in a position to-night to deal with this matter of savings banks, nor do I expect him to, but he might consider the question from all angles. The first useful purpose to be served would be the providing of facilities to people who had no other facilities, and the next purpose would be the inducing of people, even in the little communities where small sums of money are saved, to acquire habits of thrift. What has been done in other countries could be done here.
